source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood & Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design, J. Mechanical Design 133(8): design and sample
finding: Senior engineering students designed a device to harvest human power for rural communities. Examples were patents varied by distance (near/far field), commonness, and modality (picture/text).
numbers: N=153 across 9 conditions (2x2x2 plus control); assigned by seating, so cell sizes unequal. Examples were shown only after a first unaided phase.
limits: Three-way interactions have modest power. One task, one population, patents as stimuli.
agent_relevance: Same design logic fits an agent: unaided first pass, then inject sources. Do not show sources before the agent has a first attempt.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood & Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design, J. Mechanical Design 133(8): far-field effect on transfer and novelty
finding: Far-field examples were used more in solutions than near-field ones, and raised mean and max novelty versus near-field. Neither differed from the no-example control on novelty.
numbers: Transfer: p<.01, eta2=.08, d=0.60 far vs near. Mean novelty far vs near: p<.05, d=0.56, eta2=.04. Max novelty: p<.05, d=0.56. Near vs control and far vs control on novelty: n.s.
quote: solution features from near-field examples were no more likely to be present in participant solutions after processing examples
limits: Far beat near, but neither beat control alone. The effect is a contrast between two kinds of source, not proof that sources help.
agent_relevance: Compare a distant source with a near source and with no source in any internal test. Otherwise a gain may just be a near-source loss.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood & Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design, J. Mechanical Design 133(8): cost of far examples
finding: Far-field examples cost output quantity: about one fewer solution concept in the standard time. Breadth of search did not change with distance.
numbers: Quantity far vs near: p<.05, d=-0.30. Breadth by distance: p=.78. Authors state the cost is about one concept.
limits: Small effect. Far vs control on quantity not significant.
agent_relevance: Distant sources spend tokens and attention. Budget for fewer, riskier candidates, not more.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood & Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design, J. Mechanical Design 133(8): far-field raises variance in quality, not the mean
finding: Mean and max quality did not differ by distance. The spread of quality was larger with far-field examples, also larger than control.
numbers: Quality SD, far vs near d=0.64 (p<.05); far vs control d=0.78 (p<.05); eta2=.06. No effect on mean or max quality.
limits: Variance, not mean, is the benefit. It helps only if a later step can screen out the bad tail.
agent_relevance: Far sources only pay when paired with strong selection (a critic stage). Without a filter expect more bad ideas.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood & Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design, J. Mechanical Design 133(8): commonness
finding: Less-common examples gave more novel concepts than more-common ones, plus higher quality variance. More-common examples shrank quantity and breadth.
numbers: Mean novelty less vs more common: p<.01, d=0.61, eta2=.10. Breadth: more-common vs control d=-1.03 (p<.01). Quantity more-common vs control d=-0.76. Quality SD less-common vs control d=0.68.
limits: More-common examples narrowed search (a fixation effect). Less-common vs control was not significant for novelty.
agent_relevance: When retrieving sources, down-weight the most typical solution in the field. Common sources narrow the search.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood & Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design, J. Mechanical Design 133(8): far x less-common combination
finding: Only the combination of far-field and less-common examples raised novelty above the no-example control.
numbers: Dunnett post hoc vs control: mean novelty d=1.14, max novelty d=1.29. Neither factor alone differed from control.
limits: Post hoc test on collapsed modality. Large d from a single combined cell with a small N.
agent_relevance: Pick sources that are both distant in domain and rare. This is the one cell with a clear gain over no source.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood & Kotovsky (2011) On the benefits and pitfalls of analogies for innovative design, J. Mechanical Design 133(8): modality
finding: Text examples were used more in solutions than picture examples, but gave fewer concepts. Modality did not change novelty.
numbers: Transfer, text vs picture: p<.01, eta2=.09, d=0.60. Quantity text vs picture d=-0.67 (p<.01), text vs control d=-0.56.
limits: Humans only; pictures versus patent text.
agent_relevance: For an LLM the source is always text. Expect heavy copying of source wording; check for surface transfer.

source: Song, Srinivasan & Luo (2017) Patent stimuli search and its influence on ideation outcomes, Design Science 3, e25: data
finding: Undergraduates designed spherical rolling robots with patent stimuli from the home, near and far technology fields. Distance was set by position in a network of over 6 million US patents.
numbers: 138 concepts; 231 stimuli used; 242 patents provided; 121 IPC classes in 5 communities. Quality kappa=0.86 on 20 concepts.
limits: Distance at 3-digit IPC class level; one expert rated novelty; one product; students working after class.
agent_relevance: A field-style test of the same near/far question.

source: Song, Srinivasan & Luo (2017) Patent stimuli search and its influence on ideation outcomes, Design Science 3, e25: quality and novelty by field
finding: Far-only and home+far stimuli gave higher quality. Combinations including near stimuli gave higher novelty. Single-field differences were not significant.
numbers: Quality (0-2): far-only and home+far higher at 5% in most pairwise t-tests; no low-quality concepts from far-only, home+far or home+near. Novelty (0-3): near-containing combos higher at 5% vs home, far, home+far. No effect sizes reported.
limits: The authors say their quality result contradicts Fu et al. 2013 and fits Chan et al. 2011; they blame different definitions of near and far.
agent_relevance: The direction of the distance effect depends on how distance is measured. Define distance operationally before testing.

source: Song, Srinivasan & Luo (2017) Patent stimuli search and its influence on ideation outcomes, Design Science 3, e25: review of mixed prior findings
finding: The paper lists conflicting studies: Chan 2011 (far: more novelty variability, fewer concepts); Wilson 2010 (no near/far difference); Fu 2013 (near or middle stimuli gave higher max novelty and higher mean and max quality than far); Chan & Schunn 2015 (most creative solutions more often from near stimuli); Srinivasan 2017 (novelty up, quality down with patent distance).
numbers: Secondary summary; no pooled estimate given.
limits: Second-hand. I read the authors' summary, not the cited papers. I found no meta-analysis.
agent_relevance: There is no settled rule that far is better. Treat distance as a tunable setting with a middle-range default, not a maximum.

source: Chan, Dow & Schunn (2015) Do the best design ideas (really) come from conceptually distant sources of inspiration? Design Studies (search snippet only)
finding: Search snippet only; the PDF link returned 404. The snippet says support for far sources is mixed, most experiments had N<=12 per cell and only four had N>=18.
numbers: Snippet: N<=12 per cell in most studies; four studies N>=18.
limits: Not opened; do not cite numbers without reading the paper.
agent_relevance: Small-N history means the far-source advantage is not firmly estimated. Open this paper next.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur & Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining, KDD: method
finding: Learned purpose and mechanism vectors for product descriptions from crowd annotations with an RNN, then retrieved near-purpose, far-mechanism products as inspirations.
numbers: Retrieval beat TF-IDF, LSA, LDA and GloVe baselines on precision at top 1% (about 0.70 for purpose or mechanism only vs 0.63 for TF-IDF; table partly garbled in extraction).
limits: Pre-LLM model; positives were crowd labels of analogy; garbled table limits exact reading.
agent_relevance: Splitting a case into purpose and mechanism is a usable retrieval key for O7: match on purpose, vary on mechanism.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur & Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining, KDD: human ideation experiment
finding: 38 online workers redesigned products under three inspiration types. Near-purpose far-mechanism analogies gave more good ideas than surface-similar or random inspirations.
numbers: 749 ideas, 12 seed products, within-subjects. k=2 judges: P(good)=0.71 [0.48,0.87] analogy vs 0.28 TF-IDF vs 0.27 random. k=3: 0.56 vs 0.16 vs 0.14. On nine shared seeds, 46% vs 30% (surface) vs 37% (random), p<=.01. Fleiss kappa 0.51.
limits: Wide confidence intervals; authors say a replication could shrink the effect. Paid crowd workers, about 7 minutes, 1 minute unaided then 6 minutes with 12 inspirations; judged by 5 students.
agent_relevance: Strong support for 'same purpose, different mechanism' sources.

source: Hope, Chan, Kittur & Shahaf (2017) Accelerating innovation through analogy mining, KDD: surface baseline no better than random
finding: Surface-similar inspirations did not beat random ones. Both were far below the purpose-matched, mechanism-distant set.
limits: Same study, same limits.
agent_relevance: Near sources add little over random ones. Do not spend steps retrieving superficially similar cases.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR: main result
finding: Asking the model to recall relevant problems before solving beat 0-shot CoT on math, code and BIG-Bench, and was close to or above hand-written few-shot CoT.
numbers: Reported average gain +4%. GSM8K GPT-3.5-turbo: 5-shot CoT 75.0% vs self-generated exemplars 75.8% to 77.8% across variants (table rows partly garbled). Codeforces Acc@1 GPT-3.5 15% vs GPT-4 16%. BIG-Bench: 0-shot CoT 66.8% vs ours 68.4% on one task column.
limits: Gains are small on GSM8K (about 1 to 3 points). The recalled exemplars are same-domain problems, not distant sources.
agent_relevance: This is near-source self-retrieval, not distant analogy. A cheap O7 baseline whose gain over fixed few-shot is small on easy sets.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR: error analysis
finding: On 100 hand-checked GSM8K and MATH problems, solved ones mostly had relevant, correct self-generated exemplars. Unsolved ones often had good exemplars but the model could not transfer.
numbers: Of 50 solved: 35 relevant and correct, 9 relevant but wrong, 6 irrelevant. Of 50 unsolved: 28 relevant and correct yet failed (12 generalization gap, 8 over-reliance on a specific exemplar, 8 other), 12 relevant but wrong, 10 irrelevant.
quote: a generalization gap between the exemplars and the new problem
limits: N=100 hand coded by the authors; no inter-rater figure.
agent_relevance: 8 of 50 failures came from clinging to one exemplar, the fixation risk seen in Chan 2011. Ask for several sources and a check on the mapping.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR: scale boundary
finding: Self-generated exemplars help more with larger models. With smaller models, retrieved real exemplars did better.
numbers: Authors state self-generated exemplars perform better with larger-scale LLMs; few-shot with retrieved exemplars better for smaller ones (GSM8K, Table 4).
limits: Exact table cells are garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Self-generated analogies depend on model strength. Use them on the main agent; use retrieved cases for a small worker.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR: knowledge plus exemplars
finding: On Codeforces, adding generated knowledge (core concepts) to exemplars gave the best results.
numbers: Acc@1 rose from 8% (3-shot CoT) to 9% to 15% across variants; GPT-4 got 16%.
quote: knowledge act as high-level takeaways that complement low-level exemplars
limits: Very low base rates; per-variant figures partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Ask for the abstract principle, not only the example. Abstraction makes a distant source usable.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nat Hum Behav: letter strings, verbal, SAT
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat average undergraduates on letter-string and SAT-style verbal analogies.
numbers: Human N=57 (letter strings and verbal); 100 letter-string problems per type; SAT set of 374 problems (Turney), chance 20%, GPT-3 above the estimated average high-school SAT taker.
limits: Answers were scored by the authors' own rule; later tests (Lewis & Mitchell) show the result depends on familiarity.
agent_relevance: Headline strength on familiar formats. Do not read it as general analogical reasoning.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nat Hum Behav: story analogies, near vs far
finding: With Gentner's story materials GPT-3 chose the causal analogue in the near condition but not reliably in the far condition. Humans did well in both.
numbers: Humans N=54: near t(53)=21.5, far t(53)=16.7, 15/54 perfect. GPT-3: near p=.0039, far p=.065 (n.s.). Human advantage OR=0.37 for GPT-3, p=.0003. GPT-4 pilot: stronger, near perfect.
limits: GPT-3 only for the full test; GPT-4 is a supplementary check.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain mapping on causal structure is where models fail first. The same boundary appears in ARN and AnaloBench.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nat Hum Behav: Gick-Holyoak radiation problem
finding: GPT-3 used the general story to give the convergence solution when the story sat in context. With distractor stories added it lost the solution until prompted to consider the earlier stories.
numbers: Qualitative case runs; the effect mirrors the human pattern (distractors hurt, a hint restores).
limits: No fixed sample; a few prompts. GPT-3 keeps no memory across contexts.
agent_relevance: Matches the human retrieval bottleneck: a source in context is used, one buried among distractors is not. An explicit cue to look back is needed.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: On letter-string problems with permuted alphabets or symbols, humans stayed accurate while GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 dropped. The models passed comprehension checks on the new alphabets, so the drop is not a failure to understand the alphabet.
numbers: Human N=136 on Prolific; Webb's N=57. Human accuracy significantly higher than every GPT model on counterfactual alphabets (Table 2). Alternate-rule errors: 38.59% GPT-3.5, 22% GPT-4, 5.81% GPT-3.
limits: Letter strings only; Webb et al. (2024) dispute the framing (see the A02 documents). Their human accuracy was higher than in Webb's sample.
agent_relevance: A source that looks like training data is easy; a changed surface exposes the gap. Test O7 with counterfactual variants.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench: benchmarking the identification of abstract and long-context analogies
finding: Models pick analogies well for one-sentence stories but fall behind humans as stories get longer. Scale helped on short stories only.
numbers: T1 accuracy (1/10/30 sentences): GPT-4 89.1/66.5/60.7; GPT-3.5 65.3/46.4/30.8; Claude 68.2/30.2/25.9; Tulu2-70B 71.8/51.2/31.5; human 96.0/72.5/73.3. Chance 25%. 340 human-written analogies; 200-story bank for retrieval.
quote: performance plateaus across model family as model size increases
limits: Human numbers from a 50-instance annotation. Multiple choice, one correct and three distractors.
agent_relevance: Long-context distant matches are the weak spot, and a bigger model does not fix it. Compress long cases into short relational summaries before comparing.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench: human-model gap grows with length
finding: Longer stories did not hurt humans much; the human-GPT-4 gap grew from 6.9 points at one sentence to 28.8 at 30 sentences.
numbers: Gap GPT-4 vs human: 6.9 (1 sentence) vs 28.8 (30 sentences). Annotator agreement lower for long stories (about 0.70 to 0.73).
limits: Authors note subjectivity in what counts as the best analogy.
agent_relevance: A short abstraction of the case is the working unit; compare abstractions, not raw stories.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: Analogical reasoning on narratives
finding: Near analogies are solved by LLMs, far analogies are not. GPT-4 scored below chance on far analogies against near distractors.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy, chance 50%. GPT-4: near analogy 94.0 / 92.5, far analogy 57.1 / 29.1. Mean over models: near 75.0%, far 39.6%. Humans: near 97.9%, far 94.1%; overall 96.0 vs 57.3 for the LLM average.
quote: though they largely recognize near analogies, even the largest ones struggle with far analogies
limits: Column labels read from a garbled table and checked against the text.
agent_relevance: Below-chance far performance means the model prefers the surface-similar distractor. Mark surface matches as suspects.

source: Sourati et al. (2024) ARN: distractor similarity
finding: Both models and humans fell when distractors were closer to the query. Models fell more.
numbers: Humans drop slightly; models drop to below random on far analogy with a near distractor.
limits: I read the text summary, not the few-shot tables.
agent_relevance: Relational comparison must override similarity. Ask for the role mapping before the final pick.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji & Hope (2024) SciMON: scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty, ACL: retrieved inspirations
finding: A pipeline retrieved inspirations (semantic, knowledge-graph, citation neighbors) and then iteratively rewrote ideas to differ from related work. Expert raters preferred GPT-4 few-shot variants, with or without the graph.
numbers: 6 NLP graduate-level raters; 50 instances in Study I. Study II: GPT4FS+KG had more technical detail in 48% of pairs and was less incremental in 45%; the real paper idea was judged more novel and technical in 85% of comparisons.
limits: Small rater pool; generated ideas stay weaker than real papers in 85% of comparisons.
agent_relevance: Inspiration retrieval plus a novelty check improves LLM ideas, but they stay below real papers.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji & Hope (2024) SciMON: scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty, ACL: iterative novelty boosting
finding: Rewriting an idea against its nearest prior work raised novelty in about half of cases and did not lower it in the rest.
numbers: 1st iteration: 54.4% (GPT4FS), 55.6% (semantic), 47.8% (citation), 46.7% (KG) of ideas gained novelty; 2nd iteration 57.8%; 70 instances, 5 annotators.
limits: Longer ideas with generic added words such as 'novel model'; the model often combines popular concepts.
agent_relevance: Checking against the nearest known case is cheap and works about half the time. Watch for buzzword padding.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? Large-scale human study
finding: Blinded experts rated LLM-agent ideas as more novel than expert human ideas, but the LLM pool collapsed into duplicates. Not an analogy study; it sets a base rate for novelty without distant sources.
numbers: Novelty 4.84 (human, 119 reviews) vs 5.64 (AI, 109) vs 5.81 (AI + human rerank); p<.05. Excitement 4.55 vs 5.19 vs 5.46. Feasibility 6.61 vs 6.34 vs 6.44 (n.s.). Of 4000 seeds per topic only about 5% (about 200) were non-duplicates.
limits: 49 ideas per condition, 79 reviewers; short proposals; no execution test.
agent_relevance: Novelty is cheap for an LLM; diversity is the limit. A distant-source stage should aim at diversity (non-duplicates), not raw novelty scores.
